forecasts.why: The baseline has a modest pilot-only CV threshold and no heldout requirement, though inherited-code failures and unknown signal strength leave some risk.
Gradient boosting is well suited to synthetic interaction effects and pilot-only tuning, but the 0.80 CV threshold and first-run variability leave substantial failure risk.

Gradient boosting is well suited to interaction-heavy synthetic data and the CV gate favours promising settings, but the first held-out run could still miss 0.80 or breach the ±0.05 agreement bound through tuning optimism or sampling variation.

A random forest should exploit the synthetic interaction structure well enough to exceed 0.80 in pilot cross-validation, but tuning choices and sampling variation leave a meaningful chance that the first credited run falls short.
Random forests are well suited to interaction effects, but with no measured results yet, the first run must still clear both the untouched held-out AUC floor and the tight ±0.05 agreement band.

A cross-validated AUC of 0.80 is demanding for a first properly validated KNN run, and the interaction-friendly data and feature screening offer only uncertain support without any observed pilot or baseline performance.
With no performance results shown, k-nearest neighbours seems unlikely to both reach AUC 0.80 on interaction-driven data and match its cross-validated estimate within 0.05 on a single held-out run.
A first pilot-only L1 logistic fit may not capture the interaction structure well enough to reach cross-validated AUC 0.80, though tuning and feature selection leave a reasonable chance of success.

The interaction-focused setting and separate pairwise-products route suggest that plain L1 logistic regression may miss the held-out AUC floor, while the tight agreement requirement adds another way for its first run to fail.
The 0.80 CV threshold is demanding, and a logistic model on the given features may underfit interaction-driven signal despite pilot-only tuning.

The interaction-focused project and dedicated pairwise-products route suggest additive logistic regression will underfit, while the tight agreement criteria add another way for its single held-out run to fail.

The synthetic-interactions setup and interaction-specific model make the 0.80 pilot CV threshold plausible, but the absence of observed results and potential sampling or tuning variability leave meaningful uncertainty.

The pairwise-product logistic model is well matched to a synthetic interaction problem, but pairs-cv is still unreached and the first held-out run must satisfy both the AUC floor and the tight two-sided generalization-gap bound.
